Refraction is the bending of a wave — most commonly a light wave — when it passes from one material into a different material. As the wave crosses the boundary between the two materials, it changes direction. It doesn't just keep going straight; it takes a slight turn.

This bending happens because waves travel at different speeds in different materials. When a wave enters a new medium and its speed changes, that change in speed is what forces it to bend.
A Simple Way to Picture It

Imagine you're walking quickly across a smooth floor and you step diagonally onto a thick carpet. The foot that lands on the carpet first slows down, but the other foot is still moving fast on the smooth floor. This uneven slowing causes your whole body to turn — you change direction without intending to.

That is exactly what happens to a light wave during refraction. One "side" of the wave enters the new medium and slows (or speeds) while the other side hasn't yet, causing the wave to pivot.
The Critical Ingredient: An Angle

Refraction only bends a wave if the wave hits the boundary at an angle — not perfectly head-on.

If a wave hits the surface perfectly straight (perpendicular, at 90°), it still changes speed as it crosses into the new medium, but it does not change direction. It just keeps going straight, only faster or slower. No bending. No refraction.

So, two things must happen together for refraction to occur:

  1. The wave must pass into a different medium.
  2. It must hit that boundary at an angle (other than 90°).
Which Way Does It Bend?

The direction of bending depends on whether the wave is moving into a faster or slower medium.

Physicists measure this with an imaginary line drawn perpendicular to the surface at the point where the wave hits. This imaginary line is called the normal.

  • If the wave enters a slower medium (e.g., light going from air into glass), it bends toward the normal — the angle gets smaller.
  • If the wave enters a faster medium (e.g., light going from glass back into air), it bends away from the normal — the angle gets larger.

A simple memory rule: slow = toward the normal, fast = away from the normal.
How Much Does It Bend? (The Refractive Index)

Each material has a property called its refractive index (also called index of refraction). It's a number — always 1 or higher — that tells you how much that material slows down light compared to light traveling through a perfect vacuum (empty space).

  • Higher refractive index = light slows down more = more bending.
  • Lower refractive index = light slows down less = less bending.

Here are some common values:

  • Vacuum: 1.0 (light travels at its maximum speed, ~300,000 km/s)
  • Air: ~1.0003 (barely any slowing — almost identical to vacuum)
  • Water: ~1.33 (light slows to about 75% of its vacuum speed)
  • Glass: ~1.5 (light slows to about 67% of its vacuum speed)
  • Diamond: ~2.42 (light slows dramatically — this is a big reason diamonds sparkle so brilliantly)

The rule that precisely calculates the exact angle of bending using refractive indices is called Snell's Law. Without the math: the bigger the difference between the refractive indices of the two media, the sharper the bend.
Refraction and Color: Dispersion

Here is where things get beautiful.

White light (like sunlight) is not a single color — it is a mixture of all colors, each with a different wavelength. Violet light has a short wavelength; red light has a long wavelength.

When white light enters a material like glass, different colors slow down by slightly different amounts. Violet light slows a little more than red light. Because each color slows by a different amount, each color also bends by a slightly different angle.

This causes white light to fan out into a spectrum of colors — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet — each going in a slightly different direction.

This splitting of white light into its constituent colors through refraction is called dispersion.

Dispersion is why:

  • A glass prism separates sunlight into a rainbow of colors.
  • A rainbow appears in the sky — sunlight enters raindrops, bends, reflects off the back of the droplet, then bends again on the way out. Because of dispersion, each color exits at a slightly different angle, and you see the full arc of colors spread across the sky.
Everyday Examples of Refraction

1. The bent straw in a glass of water
When you put a straw in a glass of water, it looks bent or broken at the water's surface. Light from the submerged part of the straw bends as it exits the water and enters air, arriving at your eyes from a different direction than expected. Your brain, tracing that light back in a straight line, places the straw in the wrong position.

2. Pools looking shallower than they are
Light from the bottom of a swimming pool bends as it exits the water, making the bottom appear closer to the surface than it really is. A pool that looks 1 metre deep might actually be 1.33 metres deep.

3. Lenses in glasses, cameras, and microscopes
Lenses are curved pieces of glass (or other transparent material) specifically designed to refract light in controlled, useful ways. A convex (outward-curving) lens bends light inward, bringing it to a focus — used in cameras, projectors, and magnifying glasses. A concave (inward-curving) lens bends light outward, spreading it — used in glasses for nearsighted people. All of this is refraction put to work.

4. Mirages
In a desert, the air near the scorching ground is very hot and less dense, while air higher up is cooler and denser. Light from the sky bends (refracts) gradually as it passes through these layers, eventually curving upward toward your eyes. You see light from the sky appearing to come from the ground — which looks uncannily like a shimmering pool of water. No water is there; it's entirely refraction.

5. Stars appearing to twinkle
Starlight passes through layers of Earth's atmosphere at different temperatures and densities, causing continuous tiny refractions in slightly varying directions. This makes the star's image wobble rapidly, which we perceive as twinkling. Planets, being closer to us and appearing as discs rather than pinpoints, don't twinkle as much — their disc-shape averages out the wobble.

6. The sun visible after it has set
Earth's atmosphere refracts sunlight slightly around the curve of the Earth. This means you can see the sun for a minute or two even after it has geometrically dipped below the horizon. The sun you see at the exact moment of sunset is actually an optical illusion — the real sun is already below the horizon.
Refraction Is Not Just for Light

Any wave can refract when it moves between media where it travels at different speeds. Light is just the most common example.

Sound waves — Sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air. At night, the air near the ground is cooler than the air above. Sound waves traveling upward through warmer air gradually refract back downward toward the cooler surface. This is why sounds can travel surprisingly far at night — conversations, distant music, train whistles seem clearer and louder.

Water waves — Ocean waves travel faster in deep water and slower in shallow water. As a wave approaches a beach at an angle, the part of the wave reaching shallow water first slows down, causing the whole wave to gradually turn. This is why waves almost always seem to approach the shore nearly parallel to the beach, regardless of what direction they were traveling far out at sea.

Seismic waves — Earthquake waves refract as they pass through layers of the Earth with different densities. By measuring how seismic waves bend, geologists have been able to map the layers inside the Earth — the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core — without ever drilling that deep.
A Closely Related Phenomenon: Total Internal Reflection

When light travels from a denser medium (like glass) into a less dense medium (like air), and it hits the boundary at a very steep angle — beyond a certain critical angle — something interesting happens: refraction can no longer occur. Instead of bending through, all of the light bounces back inside the denser medium. This is called total internal reflection.

This is not refraction itself, but it's a direct consequence of refraction's rules, so understanding it completes the picture.

Total internal reflection is the principle behind:

  • Optical fibers: Hair-thin glass strands used to carry internet data and phone calls across continents. Light signals bounce along inside the fiber via total internal reflection, traveling enormous distances around bends without leaking out.
  • Medical endoscopes: Doctors insert flexible tubes containing optical fibers into the body to see inside, transmitting light and images using the same principle.
  • Diamond's brilliance: Diamond's exceptionally high refractive index (2.42) means total internal reflection happens at a very wide range of angles. Light that enters a diamond bounces around inside many times before it finally exits — and when it exits, dispersion spreads it into colorful flashes.
Refraction vs. Similar-Sounding Terms

These three terms are often confused:

Refraction — A wave bends because it crosses into a new medium and its speed changes. The wave continues forward, just in a new direction.

Reflection — A wave bounces back when it hits a surface, staying in the same medium (like light bouncing off a mirror). The wave does not enter the new medium.

Diffraction — A wave bends and spreads when it passes through a narrow opening or around an edge. This does not require a change of medium — it's caused by the wave's own nature, not by a speed change.
Summary

Refraction, in one precise sentence: it is the bending of a wave that occurs when it passes from one medium into another, caused by the change in the wave's speed at that boundary.

The key ideas:

  • It happens at the boundary between two different media.
  • The cause is a change in the wave's speed.
  • Entering a slower medium → bends toward the perpendicular (normal).
  • Entering a faster medium → bends away from the normal.
  • It requires the wave to hit the surface at an angle — not straight on.
  • The degree of bending depends on the refractive index of each medium.
  • Different colors (wavelengths) of light refract by slightly different amounts → dispersion → rainbows and prisms.
  • It applies to all waves: light, sound, water waves, seismic waves.
  • When refraction can no longer occur at extreme angles inside a dense medium, you get total internal reflection → optical fibers, diamond sparkle.
